name: GHK-Cu skin protocol

card.summary: Using the copper peptide GHK-Cu, topically or by injection in peptide circles, to try to improve skin quality, scarring and hair.
card.note: Injectable GHK-Cu is an unapproved research-compound use; topical GHK-Cu is a common cosmetic ingredient.

quick.overview:
GHK-Cu is a copper-binding tripeptide found in human plasma and used in cosmetics under the name copper tripeptide-1. Skin protocols built on it aim for firmer, smoother skin, better wound and post-procedure healing, and in some cases hair.

Lab studies show it stimulates collagen and glycosaminoglycan production in fibroblasts, and small human trials report anti-wrinkle and post-laser effects. Reviews note that data on skin penetration and effectiveness are limited.
quick.how: The commonly discussed route is topical serums and creams, sometimes with microneedling; some peptide communities also discuss injectable forms. Results are described over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Topical products are generally cosmetic; injected or self-compounded forms are outside approved use, with sterility and quality concerns discussed in community threads. Evidence in humans is limited.

lead: The GHK-Cu skin protocol refers to routines built around the peptide GHK-Cu (glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine bound to copper) to improve the look of skin, scars and hair. In its mainstream form it is a topical ingredient, listed on cosmetic labels as copper tripeptide-1 or GHK-Cu, in serums and creams aimed at fine lines, firmness and uneven tone.[1][11] In its looksmaxxing form it is discussed as a peptide to be microneedled in or injected, usually as one item in a wider peptide routine for skin, acne marks and recovery.[9][10][21]

The molecule was isolated from human plasma by the biochemist Loren Pickart in 1973 and identified as a tripeptide in 1977.[1][3] Its appeal for appearance rests on cell studies in which it increases collagen and glycosaminoglycan synthesis in fibroblasts, and on small cosmetic trials of creams and serums that report improvements in wrinkles, density and skin thickness.[4][5][12] A 2025 review concluded that cellular data support GHK as an anti-wrinkle ingredient, while published information on skin permeability and real-world effectiveness is insufficient.[2]

The topic reached mainstream media in 2026. NPR reported in September 2026 that the copper peptide trend had moved from creams to injections ahead of the science, and described GHK-Cu as a staple of social-media looksmaxxing content that was driving patient questions in dermatology and wellness clinics.[19] Regulators and clinicians draw a line between the topical products, which have decades of cosmetic use, and injected or compounded forms, whose human safety and efficacy data are not yet published.[19][17][18]

angle.text: Users apply it to improve fine lines, texture and recovery after resurfacing or microneedling. Some also use it on the scalp for hair thickness. Injected use is discussed mainly in peptide circles.

paras: GHK is a three-amino-acid peptide (glycine, histidine, lysine) that binds copper(II) very tightly. Wikipedia reports a high stability constant for the complex and says copper's redox activity is reportedly suppressed when it is held by GHK.[1] The peptide is found in human plasma, saliva and urine, and its reported plasma concentration falls from about 200 ng/ml at age 20 to about 80 ng/ml by age 60, a decline that proponents cite as the rationale for replacing it.[1][6]
In cosmetics the complex is sold under the INCI name copper tripeptide-1; a palmitoylated derivative, Pal-GHK, is also common in anti-wrinkle products.[2][11]

Pickart (1938-2023) began from an observation that older liver tissue behaved more like younger tissue when incubated in young donors' plasma, and in 1973 reported a plasma factor with that effect.[1][15] A 1980 Nature paper proposed that the peptide helps carry copper into cells, and through 1983-1985 his group reported accelerated wound healing and anti-inflammatory effects; patents on GHK-Cu for wound healing followed in 1988 and 1992.[16] In the 1980s Maquart and colleagues proposed that GHK works as an early repair signal because its sequence occurs in the alpha-2 chain of type I collagen, and they reported collagen stimulation in fibroblast cultures in 1988.[4][15]

The 2018 review by Pickart and Margolina, drawing on a 2010 Connectivity Map analysis, argued that GHK modulates the expression of a large share of human genes, and that this could explain its wide range of reported actions. The authors state that the meaning of many of those changes is not yet understood.[3][15] Pickart's affiliation with a skin-biology company is noted in reviews of his work.[15][16]

sections.h: Mechanism as described in the literature
paras: In cell culture, GHK-Cu at very low concentrations stimulated collagen and sulfated glycosaminoglycan synthesis, and it also increased decorin and the activity of matrix metalloproteinases together with their inhibitors, which the literature interprets as a remodelling signal.[4][5][7][1] A review of tissue-remodelling actions describes chemoattraction of repair cells, anti-inflammatory activity and stimulation of blood-vessel and nerve outgrowth.[3][8] In rats, an ischemic wound model found faster wound-size reduction with GHK-Cu than with vehicle, and connective tissue accumulation was greater in rat experimental wounds.[1][25]

Because the compound is hydrophilic, skin permeation is a recurring question: a 2025 review of liposome-encapsulated GHK-Cu notes limited passage through the stratum corneum and little published work on how well liposomes help.[22] This is why topical routines are often paired in forums with microneedling or delivery-enhanced products.[10][2]

A randomised controlled trial published in 2006 gave patients who had circumoral CO2 laser resurfacing post-treatment regimens with or without GHK-Cu and tracked erythema through healing.[12] Earlier, a 2005 study examined copper tripeptide effects on growth-factor expression in normal and irradiated fibroblasts.[20]

The Pickart and Margolina review summarises cosmetic studies that the company-affiliated authors describe as showing improved density, thickness and fine lines: a 12-week facial cream study in 71 women, a 12-week eye-cream study in 41 women compared with placebo and vitamin K cream, and an 8-week randomised double-blind nano-lipid study reporting reduced wrinkle volume versus a control serum and a peptide comparator.[15] Wikipedia describes the controlled facial trials as small and short, with a need for more research.[1] The NPR report likewise characterised human studies as mostly small, industry-funded trials of creams and serums, and said wound-healing, organ-repair and Alzheimer's findings have been in animals.[19]

Registered trials include a phase 2 study of topical GHK-Cu gel on standardised punch-biopsy wounds (NCT07437586, 60 participants, started February 2026) and a planned study of a patch's effect on circulating GHK and GHK-Cu levels (NCT07706361).[23][27] Reviews of injectable peptides in sports medicine list GHK-Cu among popular compounds and report that rigorous human safety data for unapproved peptides are scarce.[24]

Consumer-health coverage lists possible follicle blood-flow, growth-phase and thickness effects, citing a 2007 in vitro study and the Pickart reviews, and notes that human studies on hair are needed; it describes the skin evidence as stronger than the hair evidence.[11] The 2018 review lists increased hair growth and follicle size among GHK-Cu effects without a supporting study in its text.[15] NPR's summary says some small cream and serum trials have reported hair growth.[19]

sections.h: Practice as discussed in the community
paras: Topical use is the mainstream route: serums and creams applied to face or scalp, often alongside sunscreen and a moisturiser. Consumer guidance advises checking labels for copper tripeptide-1 and patch testing, and notes that some dermatology sources advise against layering with retinol, vitamin C or alpha hydroxy acids.[11]

On looksmax.org users ask whether GHK-Cu works better with microneedling; one reply says topical plus microneedling beats topical alone, and that injecting, which the poster calls pinning, beats both.[9] Another thread has an original poster with fine lines and atopic dermatitis asking whether it would make a visible difference.[10] Further threads discuss using it alongside or instead of isotretinoin, comparisons with Matrixyl, vial potency loss, reconstitution and sterility, and whether it is overhyped for acne.[21] Wellness and strength forums such as T Nation discuss pre-mixed blends such as KLOW (KPV, BPC-157, TB-500 and GHK-Cu) and GLOW stacks, with one user describing the GHK-Cu portion as the skin and hair component.[13][14][26][26] Another forum user speculated that a blend containing GHK-Cu was pulling copper into the skin and affecting other minerals, an anecdote that is unverified.[13]
These are user discussions and do not constitute clinical guidance.

The NPR report by Will Stone (7 September 2026) quoted Warren Ladiges of the University of Washington, who has studied GHK for years and sees longevity potential but said of injecting it without known effects, "I wouldn't do that to myself."[19] David Goldberg, a cosmetic dermatologist in New York, called the topical science very solid but advised holding off on injections.[19] Marisa Garshick, a dermatologist, said unregulated injectables raise doubt about whether the product is even a copper peptide.[19] Erik Marks, a nurse practitioner who occasionally offers injectable GHK-Cu, described patients with infections, injection-site irritation and elevated liver enzymes, while noting it is unclear whether the peptide caused them.[19] The report added that GHK-Cu is hard to patent, which reduces commercial incentive to fund human trials.[19]

Topical copper tripeptide-1 is sold as a cosmetic ingredient. For injectables, the FDA's compounding pages list injectable GHK-Cu among substances nominated for compounding and later withdrawn, and state the agency's concern about immunogenicity from aggregation and impurities and limited human safety data.[17] A law-firm summary reports that on 15 April 2026 the FDA announced it would remove twelve peptides including injectable GHK-Cu from Category 2, because their nominators withdrew them, and that GHK-Cu was slated for advisory committee consultation before the end of February 2027; the same summary stresses that removal from Category 2 does not make a substance eligible for compounding.[18] NPR reported that US compounding pharmacies are not technically allowed to offer GHK-Cu for human injection.[19]

Topical use rarely causes more than irritation; consumer guidance mentions allergic reactions such as redness, itching or hives and says copper toxicity from over-the-counter products is unlikely.[11] For injected product, clinicians quoted in the press cite immune reactions, copper overload, infections and uncertainty about content and sterility of online-sourced vials.[19] Wikipedia notes that GHK stimulates both metalloproteinases and their inhibitors, and advises caution about that dual action.[1]

timeline.event: Loren Pickart isolates a growth-modulating factor from human plasma albumin and reports it in Nature.[1]
The factor is identified as the tripeptide glycyl-histidyl-lysine.[1]
A Nature paper proposes GHK helps copper enter cells.[1][16]
Maquart and colleagues report collagen synthesis stimulation by GHK-Cu in fibroblast cultures.[4]
Report of stimulated glycosaminoglycan synthesis by GHK-Cu.[5]
Randomised trial of copper tripeptide skin care after CO2 laser resurfacing.[12]
Pickart and Margolina review argues GHK affects a large share of human genes.[3]
BioImpacts review finds permeability and effectiveness data for topical GHK insufficient.[2]
FDA announces removal of injectable GHK-Cu from Category 2 after withdrawn nominations; phase 2 topical wound trial begins.[18][23]
NPR reports the copper peptide trend moving from creams to injections.[19]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and peptide-minded lifting forums GHK-Cu is treated as a skin and hair peptide, often grouped with BPC-157 and TB-500 in blends.[9][10][13]

claims.claim: GHK-Cu improves skin quality, fine lines and texture.
claims.believers: Proponents point to collagen stimulation in cell studies and to users who report smoother skin after weeks of use; one thread poster asks whether it will make a visible difference to fine lines.[10][4]
claims.experts: A 2025 review concluded cell studies support GHK as an anti-wrinkle ingredient but that permeability and effectiveness data are insufficient; small short trials of creams report wrinkle improvements.[2][1]

claims.claim: Microneedling plus GHK-Cu works better than topical alone.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user says topical plus microneedling beats topical alone.[9]
claims.experts: No controlled trial of GHK-Cu combined with microneedling is cited in the reviews consulted; the permeation reviews note skin penetration is a limiting factor.[22][2]

claims.claim: Injecting GHK-Cu is more effective than topical use.
claims.believers: Forum users describe injection ('pinning') as stronger than topical or microneedling.[9]
claims.experts: NPR reported no published human studies showing injections are safe or effective; the FDA cites immunogenicity concerns for injectables.[19][17]

claims.claim: GHK-Cu helps hair growth and thickness.
claims.believers: Peptide communities and cosmetic marketing describe scalp use for follicle size and density.[11][15]
claims.experts: Consumer-health coverage says human studies on hair are needed; skin evidence is described as stronger than hair evidence.[11]

claims.claim: GHK-Cu clears acne or acne marks.
claims.believers: Forum threads ask whether to use it for acne, alongside or instead of isotretinoin, while one thread title calls it 'cope for acne'.[21][28]
claims.experts: Wikipedia and the cited reviews describe wound-healing and anti-inflammatory actions but no acne trial is cited in them.[1][3]

claims.claim: Declining GHK levels with age explain skin aging, so replacing it restores youthful skin.
claims.believers: Pickart's lineage of papers argues levels fall from about 200 to about 80 ng/ml between ages 20 and 60.[6][15]
claims.experts: The figures come from the originator's group, and reviewers of that work note the authors are affiliated with a skin-biology company and that human evidence for replacement is thin.[16]

claims.claim: Injected peptide vials from online sellers are equivalent to cosmetic GHK-Cu.
claims.believers: Users trade reconstitution and potency tips and buy blends.[21][13]
claims.experts: Dermatologist Marisa Garshick said unregulated injectables raise doubt whether the product is even a copper peptide; the FDA cites impurity and aggregation concerns.[19][17]
